title: Distilling Kimi-K3.1-Pro into Qwen3.8-27B: Teaching a model a new language
gist: Together AI used off-policy distillation to teach Qwen3.8-27B Lao: a LoRA adapter trained on ~3,800 filtered Kimi-K3.1-Pro translations lifted FLORES-200 Lao from 5.5 to 44.3 chrF++ (93% of the teacher, 92% of the gap closed) while preserving Thai, for $260 total on Together Post-Training. The key lessons: the base model's problem was language identity rather than meaning, Lao-only training collapsed Thai unless retention data was mixed in, and more teacher data beat more epochs.

insights.claim: Qwen3.8-27B, a popular small language model, answers in Thai when asked for Lao, scoring 5.5 chrF++ on FLORES-200 Lao with only 11% of outputs in Lao script, versus 47.5 for Kimi-K3.1-Pro.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Small open models have sharp blind spots on low-resource languages that larger models cover, creating demand for targeted fine-tuning.
insights.locator: While running some experiments we found out

insights.claim: A 50-sentence screen across 11 languages showed Kimi-K3.1-Pro beating Qwen3.8-27B on all of them, with Lao the largest gap (49.0 vs 7.2), followed by Northern Sotho and Zulu.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Cheap screening (50 sentences per language) is enough to locate where distillation pays off.

insights.claim: The authors frame the Lao failure as an instance of a common pattern: small models show jagged intelligence, failing a narrow task a larger, more expensive model handles easily, which distillation can fix.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Supports the business case for post-training services that close narrow gaps instead of paying frontier-model inference prices.
insights.quote: a small language model displays jagged intelligence, falling flat on a narrow task you care about while a larger, more expensive model handles it with ease
insights.locator: Admittedly, this is a niche use case

insights.claim: The base Qwen model largely preserved meaning but wrote the wrong language: its Thai output scored 64.6 on round-trip adequacy, slightly above human Lao references (64.0), so every run fixed the script within its first 25 to 50 steps.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Diagnosing whether a gap is knowledge or output-format/identity determines how cheaply it can be fixed.
insights.quote: The base model mostly had the meaning; it just wrote the wrong language.
insights.locator: The base model mostly had the meaning

insights.claim: On-policy distillation needs the teacher's log-probabilities on the student's tokens and thus a shared tokenizer, so cross-family pairs like Kimi into Qwen must use off-policy distillation, i.e. SFT on teacher-generated text.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Tokenizer compatibility constrains which teacher/student pairs can use the stronger on-policy method.

insights.claim: Off-policy distillation keeps teacher costs low because every teacher call is an ordinary serverless chat request; at $2/$10 per million input/output tokens, all 4,000 Kimi-K3.1-Pro Lao translations cost $7.46.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Synthetic training data from large open models is now very cheap, lowering the barrier to custom small models.
insights.locator: Generating data from the teacher is cheap

insights.claim: Turning thinking off improved Kimi-K3.1-Pro's Lao translation (47.3 vs 43.5 chrF++ on 300 sentences) while using about one-eighth the tokens, with Lao answers averaging about 175 output tokens.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Reasoning modes can cost more and perform worse on simple generation tasks; token-heavy reasoning is not always worth paying for.
insights.locator: Generating teacher data with serverless Kimi-K3.1-Pro

insights.claim: Kimi-K3.1-Pro's Lao was easier for the student to learn than human Lao (starting loss 0.36 vs 0.54 nats/token, ending 0.06 vs 0.16), which the authors attribute to one model's translations being more consistent than a team of human translators'.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Synthetic teacher data may be a more learnable training signal than human data, supporting synthetic-data pipelines.
insights.locator: Kimi-K3.1-Pro's Lao is easier for the student to learn

insights.claim: Fine-tuning Qwen3.8-27B on 945 human Lao references alone lifted Lao from 6.7 to 43.3 in 25 steps but collapsed Thai from 46.7 to 5.3 with 0% Thai-script output, because the model learned to write Lao whenever asked to translate.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Narrow fine-tunes can silently break adjacent capabilities; single-metric evals would pick the broken model.

insights.claim: Adding about 1,000 Kimi-K3.1-Pro Thai translations to the training mix kept Thai at 47.4 and 47.8 in the mixed runs, above the base model's 46.7, and never below 47.3 at any evaluation.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Retention data for neighboring skills is a cheap insurance policy in any custom fine-tune.

insights.claim: The authors' continual-learning rule: when teaching a model something new, mix in data that protects what it already does well and score that skill during training, since a Lao-only evaluation would have chosen the run that broke Thai.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: A practical guardrail for enterprises customizing models; evaluate regressions on adjacent tasks, not just the target.
insights.quote: when you teach a model something new, mix in data that protects what it already does well
insights.locator: This is a great point to make about continual learning

insights.claim: Expanding the Lao training set from 965 to 3,834 examples with Kimi-K3.1-Pro translations of 3,000 Wikipedia sentences raised the student from 41.9 to 44.3 chrF++, within half a point of the human-reference run but with Thai intact.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Teachers can generate unlimited data where human references are capped (FLORES dev has only 997), a structural advantage for synthetic data.
insights.locator: Closing the rest of the Lao gap

insights.claim: One epoch on 4x the teacher data reached 43.2 chrF++ versus 41.3 after three epochs of the smaller set, and training loss drops at epoch boundaries did not translate into held-out quality gains (-1 to +3 points).
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: When a student plateaus, buying more teacher data is a better spend than more GPU passes.
insights.quote: More data also beat more passes
insights.locator: More data also beat more passes

insights.claim: Distilled students score lower than human-reference-trained students on human-reference metrics partly because FLORES dev and devtest share a human translation style; scored against Kimi-K3.1-Pro's own translations, the distilled student rose from 8 to 58 chrF++ versus 47 for the human-trained one.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Benchmark scores can understate distilled models' quality; metric choice biases model comparisons.

insights.claim: A single adapter trained on 8,871 Kimi-K3.1-Pro translations across Lao, Northern Sotho, Zulu, Yoruba plus Thai improved every language, closing 87% of the Lao gap, 85% for Northern Sotho, 71% for Yoruba but only 12% for Zulu, while Thai rose to 48.0.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: One adapter can cover multiple low-resource languages, relevant to localization markets in Southeast Asia and Africa.

insights.claim: Zulu improved least because 1 to 2% of its outputs fell into repetition loops during training; the authors would first try more Zulu data or a repetition penalty.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Gap closure is uneven across languages; per-language failure analysis is needed before promising coverage.
insights.locator: Every language improved. Zulu improved least

insights.claim: All experiments in the post cost $260 on B200 GPUs via Together Post-Training; the best Lao run held its resource for 46 minutes, with steps taking a median 2.6 to 3.2 seconds at batch 16 after a 2.5 to 3 minute first step.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Closing a narrow model gap now costs hundreds of dollars, commoditizing custom-model creation and favoring platforms selling post-training compute.

insights.claim: Together Post-Training splits training between user code and GPUs: a model resource (B200s with the base model loaded) hosts a trainer running forward_backward/optim_step plus an optional generator, so one resource trains a LoRA adapter (rank 64, alpha 128, peak LR 1e-4) and samples from it for evaluation without a separate endpoint.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Sonny Khan
insights.so_what: Together is selling a low-level training API that bundles training and evaluation on one resource.
insights.locator: Training the student on Together Post-Training
